notes.claim: Good insulation shows rising resistance during the test as the charging currents disappear, while in poor insulation high leakage current hides them and the curve is much flatter.
The dielectric absorption ratio is the ratio of two time-resistance readings, such as 60 s over 30 s. The polarization index is the 10-minute reading over the 1-minute reading.
Both ratios are taken on the same equipment minutes apart, and Megger says they can be seen as independent of temperature. Your notes add that a single reading swings with conditions.
Healthy insulation shows rising resistance over time. A low or unstable PI can indicate moisture, contamination or insulation breakdown.
Your notes rate PI below 1 poor, 1 to 2 questionable, 2 to 4 okay and above 4 good, and DAR below 1.25 inadequate, 1.25 to 1.6 satisfactory and above 1.6 excellent.
Makers' bands differ from the notes' names and cut-offs, so the client's criteria decide pass or fail.
notes.contested: Your notes rate PI 1 to 2 questionable and DAR 1.25 to 1.6 satisfactory. A Megger Q&A says PI of 2.0 or higher and DAR of 1.4 or higher indicate good insulation, and Megger accepts PI of 1 to 2 for very low-capacitance equipment.

notes.claim: Megger says the DAR reading is usually lower than the PI reading because its test times are shorter.
Your notes pass an IR test if the voltage is held for the full duration and the resistance exceeds the client's criteria, and say to default to PI or DAR when possible.
After the test the cable is discharged: check the device display, use the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then apply earths to core and screen. Your notes allow 5 times the charging time.
notes.contested: Your notes say to allow 5 times the charging time to discharge, without defining it. Megger's guide says to discharge for about four times as long as the test voltage was applied.

notes.claim: Megger's guide gives the discharge time as about four times as long as the test voltage was applied in a previous test.

Megger's guide says to discharge the item under test for five times as long as it was tested, and gives the example of a 10-minute PI test, which needs 50 minutes. A Fluke application note says about five times the testing charge time.
Megger's guide says to short out a tested item firmly after discharge until it is needed, because stored absorption charge can be released afterwards and raise the voltage to dangerous levels.

Megger's guide uses charging time in a second sense, the time the test set takes to charge the sample, which follows from the sample's capacitance. It is a separate idea from the five times rule, which counts the time the voltage was applied.
notes.contested: Your notes say five times the charging time without defining it. Megger's newer guide says five times as long as the item was tested, with 50 minutes after a 10-minute PI test, and a Fluke application note says about five times the testing charge time. Megger's older guide says about four times. The lesson uses five times the time the voltage was applied.

notes.claim: Megger puts the positive terminal on the grounded outside of a cable, so the negative lead goes to the conductor. For a plain IR test it says polarity rarely matters, but on older insulation electroendosmosis gives a lower reading when the positive terminal is on the grounded side.
The current in an IR test is a charging current and an absorption current, which fall to negligible values, and a small steady leakage current that is left.

A single IR reading falls markedly as temperature rises, with a rule of thumb of halving for every 10 degrees C. A time-resistance ratio such as PI is relatively independent of temperature and needs no past records.
A PI or DAR close to 1 means the insulation is judged to have deteriorated.
Some materials show very little or no dielectric absorption, and a high PI above 5 may point to brittle or cracked insulation, so a PI is read with the material in mind.
IEEE 43 (a rotating-machine practice) says the PI test is not recommended as an assessment tool when the 1-minute reading is above 5000 megohms. A long XLPE cable can read far above that.
notes.contested: Your notes and Megger use PI on cables with no upper limit. IEEE 43 is written for rotating machines, not cables, and a Fluke note says cabling shows little absorption current. The lesson teaches PI as the notes do, flags that a very high 1-minute reading makes the ratio hard to trust, and leans on the client's criterion and the trend.

notes.claim: Megger's Table I rates DAR (60/30 s) 1.0 to 1.25 questionable, 1.4 to 1.6 good and above 1.6 excellent, with a gap between 1.25 and 1.4, and PI below 1 dangerous, 1 to 2 questionable, 2 to 4 good and above 4 excellent. A Megger Q&A calls PI of 2.0 or higher and DAR of 1.4 or higher good.
notes.contested: Your notes name the PI bands poor, questionable, okay, good and set DAR at 1.25 and 1.6 with no gap. Megger's names and DAR cut-offs differ. Teach the notes' bands for the practice, show Megger's as a maker's view, and let the client's criterion settle pass or fail.

notes.claim: Megger says diagnostic testers for medium-voltage cables, machines and transformers normally have outputs of 5 or 10 kV, so a 5 kV IR test on a 66 kV cable is a normal diagnostic test voltage.
Every insulation test starts from fully discharged insulation.
